figures.caption: Figure 1: What should an EEG pretext task predict? LaBraM predicts discrete codes from a separately trained vectorquantized tokenizer; CBraMod, CSBrain and REVE reconstruct the raw waveform of masked patches. SpecBraM keeps the masked-patch setting but changes the target: it regresses the log spectral energy of each masked patch in a few fixed frequency bands. The bottom row shows the filterbank-tokenizer variant; the main model uses a plain linear patch embedding. In our experiments the effect of the target is larger than that of the tokenizer (Sec. 6).

Table 1: Pretext-target study at matched backbone, data (2,388 h), steps (16 epochs) and launcher; only the target (or, last row, the mask axis) changes. Filterbank tokenizer; strict linear probe, mean±std over three pretraining seeds. “1%”: balanced accuracy with 1% of the labelled training epochs (mean of five subsets). ∆: difference to the band-power row in balanced-accuracy points.

Table 4: Strict linear probe on sleep staging. Frozen encoder, mean-pooled features, logistic regression with C selected on the validation split, test scored once (deterministic); a 30-s epoch is the mean of its three 10-s window features. Every model we ran sees the identical epochs and splits, each in its own input convention (Sec. 5). SpecBraM rows: mean±std over three pretraining seeds. †Quoted from the REVE paper (its own linear-probing protocol). Handcrafted rows: features averaged over the three 10-s windows of each epoch (as for every encoder; better than whole-epoch features), same samples and probe; ∗1-Hz log PSD (0.5–45 Hz), relative power in six bands, Hjorth parameters, spectral entropy, 95% spectral edge, line length and kurtosis per channel.

Table 5: Label efficiency (strict linear probe, balanced accuracy vs. fraction of labelled training epochs; <100%: mean of five fixed random subsets shared by all models). Our rows: mean over three pretraining seeds.

Table 6: Sleep staging, fine-tuned (5-class, 30-s epochs in sequences of 20, one shared 1-layer sequence transformer; identical subject-disjoint splits as Zhou et al. (2025)). Baselines as reported by Zhou et al. (2025) (REVE: its paper, ISRUC only). Our rows: mean±std over three pretraining seeds (one fine-tuning run each), so the spread includes pretraining variance, unlike the baselines’ fine-tuning-seed spread.

Table 7: Strict linear probe beyond sleep: binary tasks. Samples, channels and subject-disjoint splits are produced by CBraMod’s own preprocessing scripts, so every model is probed on identical samples. Mental Arithmetic (MA) has only 4 test subjects. †CBraMod’s fine-tuned result from its paper, for reference.

Table 8: Strict linear probe beyond sleep: multi-class tasks (protocol as Table 7). FACED: 9-class emotion (chance 0.111); PhysioNet-MI: 4-class motor imagery (chance 0.25). ‡CBraMod with a frozen backbone and a trained classifier, from its paper (Table 18). †CBraMod fine-tuned, from its paper.

Table 9: SEED-VIG vigilance regression (PERCLOS) on the split stated in the CBraMod paper (experiments 1–15/16–19/20– 23 in subject order). Linear probe = frozen encoder + ridge regression (regularization on validation R2); FT = full fine-tuning (MSE, epoch selected on validation R2). Input band 0.5–45 Hz (standard) or 4–45 Hz (high-passed; the cutoff the validation split selects for both linear-tokenizer targets). Our rows: mean±std over three pretraining seeds. †From the CBraMod paper.
